families.outcome: Choose and justify a route for preparing a named pure dry salt from an acid and a base
families.context: A school preparation of copper(II) sulfate and of zinc sulfate, start to finished crystals

variants.variation: choose the first stage when the base is insoluble — the case the existing bank teaches wrongly
variants.misconception: believes an insoluble base rules the route out, when insolubility is exactly what makes the excess filterable; also that copper metal reacts with dilute sulfuric acid

variants.variation: reverse it — given four salts, decide which one forces a titration
variants.misconception: thinks the method is decided by the salt rather than by whether the base dissolves

variants.variation: produce the method name from a description of the constraint, with no options to choose from
variants.misconception: reaches for 'add excess and filter' whatever the reactants are

variants.variation: diagnose a plausible mistake from an observation — blue filtrate, white solid
variants.misconception: reads 'dry sample' as 'heat until nothing is left', driving off the water of crystallisation

variants.variation: compare two pupils' plans for the same salt and decide which can give a pure product
variants.misconception: thinks using a reactant up completely is the tidier plan, missing that the leftover must be one you can remove

families.outcome: Apply solubility rules to prepare an insoluble salt by precipitation and to judge when that route is available
families.context: Mixing two solutions to precipitate a named insoluble salt, then filtering, washing and drying it

variants.variation: select the pair of starting solutions, given the solubility rule in the stem
variants.misconception: picks any two substances containing the right elements, without checking both are soluble enough to be solutions

variants.variation: name the product — requires swapping partners and then applying the rule, with nothing to choose between
variants.misconception: names the salt that stayed dissolved instead of the one that came out

variants.variation: justify a step of the procedure rather than choose the procedure
variants.misconception: believes filtering alone gives a pure solid — it separates solid from liquid, not solid from dissolved solid

variants.variation: always / sometimes / never on a generalisation about one metal's salts
variants.misconception: treats solubility as a property of the metal rather than of the whole salt

families.outcome: Decide what a temperature rise can and cannot show about heat released, and which variables must be controlled
families.context: Neutralisation reactions in a cup, compared by temperature rise — the direct correction of g9s-inq-c100

variants.variation: reversed — given the rise and the final reading, find the starting temperature
variants.misconception: adds the rise to the final reading, producing a start hotter than the finish

variants.variation: name the condition that must hold before the largest rise may be called the most heat
variants.misconception: reads the biggest number straight off as the biggest heat, ignoring mass of solution and heat loss — the exact flaw the audit found in g9s-inq-c100

variants.variation: resolve two careful results that appear to contradict (6.4 °C against 3.2 °C)
variants.misconception: assumes equal volumes make an experiment fair, forgetting concentration decides how much actually reacts

variants.variation: state the uncontrolled variable, with volume already ruled out in the stem
variants.misconception: lists only the quantity physically measured out (volume) as the thing to keep the same

variants.variation: two start/finish pairs whose rises are equal though the final readings are not
variants.misconception: compares final temperatures instead of rises, and calls the hotter finish the bigger reaction

families.outcome: Place an unknown metal in the reactivity series from test results, and predict displacement from that position
families.context: An unnamed metal tested against cold water, steam, dilute acid and three sulfate solutions

variants.variation: place the metal from three results, one of which is a non-reaction
variants.misconception: uses only the positive result and ignores what the metal failed to react with

variants.variation: place it from one displacement that happens and one that does not — both bounds needed
variants.misconception: treats the failed displacement as no information, when it fixes the upper bound

variants.variation: predict how many of three parallel tests react, and give the reason
variants.misconception: expects a reactive-looking metal to react with everything, rather than judging pair by pair

variants.variation: explain a NON-reaction by naming what copper must sit below
variants.misconception: answers 'zinc' — true but explains nothing, since many metals below zinc still fizz in acid

families.outcome: Balance equations by coefficients only, and check that the formulae themselves are right first
families.context: Equations drawn from reactions this course already uses — aluminium and chlorine, iron oxide reduction, water, limestone and acid

variants.variation: supply the missing coefficient from the product side
variants.misconception: writes 1 because the reactant formula shows a single atom

variants.variation: same shape, but the blank is on a reactant that carries two different elements
variants.misconception: balances carbon and stops, without checking oxygen then works out

variants.variation: count atoms rather than supply a coefficient — the element appears in two substances
variants.misconception: counts only the substance whose name contains 'oxide' and answers 3 instead of 6

variants.variation: diagnose a pupil's balancing method that gives a numerically balanced but chemically wrong equation
variants.misconception: changes a subscript to balance, turning water into hydrogen peroxide

variants.variation: convert a word equation and pick the one that is both correctly formulated and balanced
variants.misconception: balances an equation whose formulae are already wrong (CaCl, Ca₂CO₃)

families.outcome: Build a formula by cancelling ionic charges, keeping polyatomic groups whole
families.context: Ion charges supplied in every stem, so no memorised table is needed

variants.variation: straight application with two simple ions
variants.misconception: writes the charges in reading order and gets Al₃O₂ instead of Al₂O₃

variants.variation: produce the formula, and the anion is a group that must be bracketed
variants.misconception: writes CaNO32 or CaN2O6, breaking the nitrate group apart

variants.variation: reversed and extended — deduce the metal's charge from one formula, then use it in another compound
variants.misconception: carries the subscript across from the sulfate to the chloride and writes M₂Cl

variants.variation: correct a given wrong formula rather than build one from scratch
variants.misconception: pairs one ion with one ion regardless of charge, leaving the compound charged

families.outcome: Choose a separation technique, and order two techniques when more than one product must be kept
families.context: Recovering substances from salt water and from a two-liquid mixture

variants.variation: name the technique for a single named product
variants.misconception: answers 'filtration' — a filter stops undissolved bits, but dissolved salt passes through

variants.variation: name the technique from a description of the procedure, where the SOLID is what is kept
variants.misconception: confuses it with distillation, which is used when the liquid is the wanted product

variants.variation: sequence two techniques under a constraint — BOTH products must be recovered
variants.misconception: treats evaporating as equivalent to distilling, losing the water it was supposed to keep

variants.variation: correct a claim about which fraction distils first, given a boiling point in the stem
variants.misconception: thinks the liquid present in the larger amount comes over first

families.outcome: Interpret rainwater pH data around a pollution source, and separate a supported conclusion from a causal claim
families.context: Four rainwater pH readings at measured distances upwind and downwind of a coal-burning power station

variants.variation: name the pollutant that connects the fuel to the data
variants.misconception: answers carbon dioxide, which acidifies rain naturally but is not what makes it unusually acidic here

variants.variation: apply a threshold given in the stem to four readings
variants.misconception: calls anything below pH 7 acid rain, when clean rain is already 5.6

variants.variation: choose the conclusion the four readings actually support, including one option about a variable never measured
variants.misconception: states a conclusion beyond the data (seasonal output, or all four samples being acid rain)

variants.variation: identify the missing information before a causal claim can be made
variants.misconception: treats a strong spatial correlation as proof of cause

families.outcome: Process a carbon dioxide and temperature record, and judge what kind of evidence would support a causal claim
families.context: Atmospheric CO₂ at 350 ppm in 1988 and 420 ppm in 2023, with mean global temperature over the same years

variants.variation: read the change out of two values
variants.misconception: quotes the final value instead of the difference

variants.variation: same two values, now as a percentage increase
variants.misconception: divides by the final value (16.7%) instead of the original (20%) — percentage increase against percentage of the final amount

variants.variation: say what two rising records, on their own, establish
variants.misconception: reads correlation as proof of causation; or dismisses a comparison because the units differ

variants.variation: rank competing evidence — mechanism, more correlation, opinion, authority. Written against the audit's g9s-inq-c042 finding, so every wrong option is genuinely tempting rather than obviously silly
variants.misconception: ranks evidence by how many people, or how important a body, states it

families.outcome: Choose a neutralising substance for a real situation, taking the constraint of the situation into account
families.context: Indigestion, acidic farmland, and insect stings of opposite pH

variants.variation: select the neutraliser for a named everyday use
variants.misconception: picks a salt (sodium chloride), which is the product of neutralisation and cannot neutralise anything

variants.variation: produce the substance name from its source and its purpose
variants.misconception: names a fertiliser, which feeds the crop but does nothing about acidity

variants.variation: explain why the chemically better performer is rejected — the constraint decides, not the chemistry
variants.misconception: assumes the fastest or most complete reaction is always the one chosen

variants.variation: change one condition (acidic sting to alkaline sting) and predict the outcome of the same treatment
variants.misconception: applies a rule where its condition does not hold — 'baking soda soothes stings' is true only for the acidic kind

families.outcome: Compare two metals in acid fairly, and read a gas-collection record correctly
families.context: Zinc and magnesium in dilute acid, first unfairly and then fairly, with hydrogen collected in a syringe

variants.variation: state the identifying test for the gas produced
variants.misconception: offers the limewater test, which detects carbon dioxide from a carbonate, not hydrogen from a metal

variants.variation: identify the uncontrolled variable behind a conclusion that is the wrong way round
variants.misconception: reads reaction speed straight off as reactivity, ignoring surface area (powder against strip)

variants.variation: same experiment with the control fixed — say what may now be concluded, overturning the earlier answer
variants.misconception: holds on to the conclusion from the unfair test instead of discarding it

variants.variation: read a gas syringe at two times and find the volume produced in the second interval
variants.misconception: quotes the second reading (42) as the interval volume, treating a running total as a rate

needs.problem: The stem asserts a factual error: 'She cannot use copper hydroxide because it is insoluble.' Insoluble bases are precisely what the excess-solid route uses — Cu(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + 2H₂O works, and the keyed answer's own method (excess copper(II) OXIDE, also insoluble) contradicts the stem's premise inside the same item.
needs.fix: Replace the second sentence of the stem with a premise that is true, e.g. 'She has copper(II) hydroxide, which is insoluble in water.' and leave the options as they are. The keyed answer stays correct; only the false justification has to go. If a reason for rejecting Cu(OH)₂ is wanted at all, there is none at this level — it is a perfectly good starting material.
needs.doNotEdit: Left untouched per the isolation rules. g9s-cfam-001-a and -b teach the correct rule (the choice depends on whether the BASE dissolves, not on the salt) without touching this file.

needs.problem: ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is a mechanical one, not a wording one. The `answer` string ('Excess acid (or excess base) will contaminate the final salt product and make it impure') is NOT one of the four strings in `options` — the option reads 'Excess reactant will contaminate…'. makeMCQ() filters options by `o !== answer`, keeps a random 3 of the 4, and then prepends the answer. So the item is dealt with the answer PLUS three of the four original options, and the near-identical 'Excess reactant will contaminate…' appears alongside the keyed answer 75% of the time. That is the audit's 'two equivalent correct statements'.
needs.fix: Make `answer` byte-identical to options[0] ('Excess reactant will contaminate the final salt product and make it impure'). No option text needs to change.
needs.worthChecking: This failure mode is silent — scripts/test-option-parity.js passes, because makeMCQ guarantees the answer is present by construction. A cheap new check would be: for every source item, assert `options.includes(answer)` BEFORE the factory runs. Nothing in the repo does that today, and any other item with a mistyped answer string has the same defect.

notes: 47 items, all subsections taken from tmp/family-expansion/declared-subsections.json (the manifest), never from pack-map.json's tag list — no new subsection-invariant failure. HTML entities were deliberately avoided in option text: scripts/test-option-parity.js decodes only a fixed table, and ₂ (₂) falls through to '?', which would have made Al₂O₃ / Al₃O₂ / Al₂O₂ read as three identical options and failed the duplicate-option check. Literal Unicode subscripts are used instead, as the rest of the pack does. Measured for this batch: 29 four-option MCQs, 0 duplicate-option sets, 0 items where the answer is materially the longest option, average within-question spread 4.0 chars (pack baseline 14.6, real-paper target 6.5-6.8). Pack-level effect: answer-visibly-longest 35.7% → 34.4%, spread 14.6 → 14.2, flagged items unchanged at 119 (all pre-existing). Every numeric answer re-derived by hand: 22.4 / 0 / 2 / 3 / 6 / 70 / 20 / 24. Every equation re-balanced by hand.
